hume-1779-dialogues.title: Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion
hume-1779-dialogues.summary: Hume's posthumous dialogue on what reason can tell us about God. Cleanthes argues from the design of the world to a divine mind like our own, Demea defends faith and the a priori proof, and the sceptic Philo picks both apart, ending on the problem of evil.
hume-1779-dialogues.source: Hume, David. *Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion*. 2nd ed. London, 1779.
hume-1779-dialogues.copyright: Hume’s text is in the public domain: he died in 1776, and the *Dialogues* were first published in 1779. The transcription is adapted from Wikisource, by Wikisource contributors, and is available under the [Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 License](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/).

hume-1777-enquiry.title: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding
hume-1777-enquiry.summary: Hume's recasting of the first book of his Treatise: where our ideas come from, why our expectations from experience rest on custom rather than reason, what necessary connexion and liberty amount to, why testimony can never establish a miracle, and what a mitigated scepticism leaves us with.
hume-1777-enquiry.source: Hume, David. *Enquiries Concerning the Human Understanding and Concerning the Principles of Morals*. Edited by L. A. Selby-Bigge. 2nd ed. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1902.
hume-1777-enquiry.copyright: In the public domain. Hume died in 1776, and the *Enquiry* is given in the posthumous edition of 1777. Selby-Bigge’s 1902 edition is out of copyright too: he died in 1951, more than 70 years ago.

nova-kepleriana-4.title: Die Keplerbriefe auf der Nationalbibliothek und auf der Sternwarte in Paris
nova-kepleriana-4.summary: The Latin texts of Kepler’s letters to Johann Seussius and Philipp Müller (1622–1630) found in Paris by Walther von Dyck, with letters of Kepler’s son-in-law Jacob Bartsch and the Danzig astronomer Peter Crüger on the Rudolphine Tables, the Ephemerides, Kepler’s death and the fate of his papers, from Nova Kepleriana 4 (1927).
nova-kepleriana-4.source: Dyck, Walther von, and Max Caspar, eds. *Die Keplerbriefe auf der Nationalbibliothek und auf der Sternwarte in Paris*. Nova Kepleriana: Wieder aufgefundene Drucke und Handschriften von Johannes Kepler 4. Abhandlungen der Bayerischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, Mathematisch-naturwissenschaftliche Abteilung 31, no. 1. Munich: Verlag der Bayerischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1927.
nova-kepleriana-4.transcribed_from: a digital facsimile of the 1927 edition (ISBN 978-3-486-75614-2). The Bavarian Academy of Sciences also has it [online](https://publikationen.badw.de/de/003071295).
nova-kepleriana-4.copyright: Only public-domain texts from this edition are reproduced here: the letters of Kepler, Bartsch, Crüger and Müller (1620–1635), in the Latin of the 1927 edition, and Walther von Dyck’s preface and introduction (von Dyck died in 1934, more than 70 years ago). Max Caspar’s German translations and the editors’ notes and commentary are left out: Caspar died in 1956, so they remain in copyright until 1 January 2027.

alexis-1558-secretes.title: The Secretes of Alexis of Piemount
alexis-1558-secretes.summary: The first part of the most popular book of secrets of the sixteenth century, in William Ward's first English translation: six books of remedies, perfumes, confections, cosmetics, colours and dyes, and the working of metals and counterfeit stones, gathered, so the aged Alexis claims, over a lifetime of travel and kept secret until remorse moved him to publish them.
alexis-1558-secretes.source: Alexis of Piemont. *The Secretes of the Reuerende Maister Alexis of Piemount*. Translated by William Ward. London: John Kingstone for Nicolas Inglande, 1558.
alexis-1558-secretes.transcribed_from: the [Text Creation Partnership’s keyboarded edition](https://github.com/textcreationpartnership/A16068) (EEBO-TCP A16068). Every page links to its image in the [Internet Archive’s scan](https://archive.org/details/bim_early-english-books-1475-1640_the-secretes-of-the-reve_ruscelli-girolamo_1558) of the 1558 edition.
alexis-1558-secretes.copyright: In the public domain: the book was printed in 1558. The TCP transcription is released under [CC0 1.0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/).

bacon-1620-novum-organum.title: Novum Organum
bacon-1620-novum-organum.subtitle: or, True Suggestions for the Interpretation of Nature
bacon-1620-novum-organum.summary: Bacon's new instrument for the sciences, in two books of aphorisms. The first clears the ground: the idols that beset the mind, the faults of the received philosophy, and the grounds for hope in a new method. The second sets out that method, a true induction rising by degrees from tables of instances to the forms of things, worked through on the nature of heat, with the twenty-seven kinds of prerogative instances.
bacon-1620-novum-organum.source: Bacon, Francis. *Novum Organum*. Edited by Joseph Devey. New York: P. F. Collier & Son, 1902. First published in Latin, London, 1620.
bacon-1620-novum-organum.transcribed_from: the [Project Gutenberg text](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/45988) (eBook #45988), by Jana Srna, Marie Bartolo, Bryan Ness and the Online Distributed Proofreading Team. Roman numerals replaced with Arabic numerals.
bacon-1620-novum-organum.copyright: In the public domain. Bacon died in 1626, and Joseph Devey, the editor, in 1897; this printing was published in the United States in 1902. The Gutenberg text is in the public domain in the USA.

kepler-1630-admonitio.title: Admonitio ad astronomos
kepler-1630-admonitio.subtitle: On the rare and wonderful phenomena of the year 1631
kepler-1630-admonitio.author: Jacob Bartsch
kepler-1630-admonitio.summary: Kepler's notice that Venus and Mercury would both cross the face of the Sun in 1631, with his call to astronomers everywhere to watch for them, excerpted from his Ephemeris and published by his son-in-law Jacob Bartsch, whose letters to Philipp Müller, address to the reader and calculations surround it in this second printing.
kepler-1630-admonitio.source: Bartsch, Jacob, ed. *Admonitio ad astronomos, rerumque coelestium studiosos, de raris mirisque anni 1631 phaenomenis, Veneris puta et Mercurii in Solem incursu*, by Johannes Kepler. Frankfurt: Godefrid Tampach, 1630. First published at Leipzig, 1629.
kepler-1630-admonitio.transcribed_from: the [page images](https://archive.org/details/den-kbd-pil-20002499-001/mode/2up) of the copy in the Royal Library, Copenhagen (KB 52,94).
kepler-1630-admonitio.copyright: In the public domain. Kepler died in 1630 and Bartsch in 1633.
